records.name_note: Admissible dedicated single-species pages split on lead name. MoBot's dedicated page carries a single structured value, 'Common Name: hazel alder'. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized — Alder, Hazel Alder, Smooth Alder, Tag Alder — and reproduces the parenthetical in its page heading, so its order does not rank the names; NC State's description prose instead uses 'Hazel alder' throughout. 'Alder' is excluded as a genus-umbrella name (MoBot: 'Genus name is the Latin name for alder.'). RHS's page title and profile subtitle lead with 'smooth alder' ('Alnus serrulata | smooth alder'), listing 'hazel alder' under its separate 'Other common names' field. 'Tag Alder' (the name this batch was researched under) sits in NC State's four-entry list and opens MoBot's descriptive prose ('Alnus serrulata, commonly called tag alder, smooth alder or hazel alder, ...'), but heads no source's structured common-name field or page title. Hazel Alder is used as common_name on MoBot's single-value Common Name field and NC State's body prose.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: none of the three admissible pages found (NC State Plant Toolbox, MoBot Plant Finder, RHS) carry any poison/toxicity information for Alnus serrulata — NC State's structured field set for this page contains no Poison Part or Poison Severity fields at all.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field gives Acid (<6.0) [open-ended, no floor] and Neutral (6.0-8.0) [closed band], but RHS's pH field lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' as acceptable — since RHS admits alkaline soils, soil_ph_max is left null, and since it also admits acid soils (consistent with NC State's open-ended acid band), soil_ph_min is left null too.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives an explicit watering statement for this species. MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium to wet' field is a disclosed counterpoint (mid-scale-to-wet), not a watering instruction, so it was not used as the basis for keep_moist or any other token.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength left null: RHS's cultivation note says the plant needs 'very little fertility' because of nitrogen-fixing root nodules, but no source gives a species-specific fertilizer schedule, dilution strength, or active months, and no genus-level crop-production page was used per the rules.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis all left null: this is an in-ground native wetland shrub/small tree, not a houseplant or container plant, and no admissible source frames its care in these terms.

outdoor_sun_exposure limited to full_sun and part_shade: NC State's Light field (Full sun; Partial Shade), MoBot's Sun field ('Full sun to part shade') and RHS's Position field ('Full sun, Partial shade') all converge on exactly these two values; no source's structured field supported part_sun or full_shade for this species.

soil_drainage=moisture_retentive is based on two independent cultivation-requirement statements: RHS's Cultivation section ('Needs good light, permanently damp soil...') and NC State's own body-prose cultivation sentence ('requires full sun to partial shade in moist to wet soils with a neutral pH'), corroborated (not contradicted) by NC State's structured Soil Drainage field values 'Moist' and 'Occasionally Wet' (not the Good Drainage + Moist pair that would indicate moderate). RHS's separate structured Moisture field ('Moist but well-drained or Poorly-drained') and its 'Drought Resistance: Yes' tag are disclosed tolerance/alternate-condition data, not used as the basis.

soil_base=garden_bed inferred from RHS listing in-ground garden soil types (Chalk, Clay, Loam, Sand) and NC State's Landscape Location tags (Naturalized Area, Pond, Riparian, Slope/Bank) — no admissible source frames this as a container/potting-mix plant.

No admissible source (hgic.clemson.edu, edis.ifas.ufl.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, extension.psu.edu, extension.umd.edu, fieldreport.caes.uga.edu) has a dedicated single-species page for Alnus serrulata; all mentions found there were within multi-species lists or unrelated publications (e.g., UF/IFAS's ENH229/ST070 page is for Alnus glutinosa, a different species, and was excluded).

common_name researched as Tag Alder; landed as Hazel Alder on MoBot's single-value Common Name field and NC State's body prose (RHS leads with smooth alder; the split is disclosed in name_note). No other Alnus is in this catalog.

records.name_note: Sources split on which name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) list has two entries, "Chokeberry" then "Red Chokeberry", in the same order as the page title parenthetical "(Chokeberry, Red Chokeberry)"; NC State's body prose ties the name to the fruit ("The fruits are edible but so astringent that they may cause choking (hence the common name).") without qualifying which chokeberry. MoBot's "Common Name:" field shows the single value "chokeberry", while MoBot's own prose calls the plant "commonly called red chokeberry". Penn State Extension's article is titled "Rain Garden Plants: Red Chokeberry" and RHS's species page is titled "Aronia arbutifolia | red chokeberry". Because the unqualified "Chokeberry" does not distinguish this species from its genus-mates while "Red Chokeberry" is the name two dedicated pages lead with and two sources' prose uses, common_name is set to Red Chokeberry. Distinct from Aronia melanocarpa (Black Chokeberry) already in this catalog.
unknowns: Clemson HGIC, UGA fieldreport.caes.uga.edu, ask.ifas.ufl.edu, and edis.ifas.ufl.edu were searched but returned no dedicated page for Aronia arbutifolia (Clemson's chokeberry factsheet URL 404s; UF/IFAS searches surfaced only unrelated species), so those domains contribute no fields here.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null: NC State's page carries no Poison block at all (no severity, symptoms, toxic principle, or poison-part list), and no admissible source states any hazard scoped to cats or dogs.

Fruit edibility (human/wildlife, not pet-toxicity) is documented but has no schema field: NC State states 'The fruits are edible but so astringent that they may cause choking (hence the common name). The red chokeberry's fruits can be used in canning or making jams and jellies'; MoBot notes fruits 'are sometimes used to make tasty jams and jellies'; Penn State Extension notes 'Berries are eaten by mammals and some birds' and that deer browse the shrub.

water_regime left null: Penn State's only moisture-framing statement is its rain-garden 'Hydrologic zone' siting label ('Moist, can tolerate occasional periods of wet soil'), which describes stormwater-basin siting rather than a cultivation watering instruction; MoBot's structured Water field reads only 'Medium' (mid-scale, does not support keep_moist per rules); no admissible source gives an unambiguous watering-cadence statement for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's Light field values ('Full sun (6 or more hours...)', 'Partial Shade (...2-6 hours)') are the site-wide light-category legend definitions, not species-specific prose, per instructions.

No admissible source provided indoor-climate fields (day/night temperature, humidity, foot-candle light levels, chill-damage onset), fertilizer schedule/strength, or watering day-intervals for this in-ground, cold-hardy (USDA zones 3a-9b) native shrub, so those fields are left null.

soil_base is set to garden_bed as an inference that this is an in-ground landscape/native shrub (NC State: Native Plant, Shrub, planting-space field in feet) rather than any potting or container medium; no admissible source frames it as container-grown.

RHS's species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/1609/aronia-arbutifolia/details, title 'Aronia arbutifolia | red chokeberry') was located by the auditor after the research pass reported only the 'Brilliantissima' cultivar page; its Name Status, pH, Cultivation, Position and Moisture fields are cited above.

records.name_note: Three admissible sources agree on the common name, with no split. NC State's Common Name(s) list holds a single entry, 'Swamp Rose,' matching the page title's parenthetical '(Swamp Rose)' and the body prose, which opens 'Swamp rose is a deciduous shrub in the rose family (Rosaceae).' MoBot's Common Name field carries the single value 'swamp rose', with no additional common-name control on the page. RHS's plant-profile subtitle, also carried in the page title 'Rosa palustris | swamp rose', likewise gives 'swamp rose', and the RHS page has no 'Other common names' section. No admissible source used 'Marsh Rose' for this species. Distinct from Rosa rugosa (Rugosa Rose) already in this catalog.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: NC State's Problems field for this species carries only "Spines/Thorns" (no Poisonous Plant Type tag, no Poison block), and no admissible source discusses toxicity to cats or dogs specifically for Rosa palustris.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field reads "Acid (<6.0)", an open-ended band with no closed floor or ceiling, so no numeric bound can be set; MoBot's Culture and Noteworthy Characteristics sections describe the soil only as "acidic"/"organically rich" prose, not a numeric pH range, and RHS's page for this species has no Soil or pH field at all to check in either direction.

soil_drainage moderate: NC State's structured Soil Drainage field, cited first, lists Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Wet -- the Good Drainage + Moist pair this catalog reads as moderate. Both sources' cultivation prose calls for boggy soils (NC State 'It is best grown in full sun and in acidic, boggy soils that are high in organic matter.'; MoBot 'Best grown in acidic, organically rich, boggy to wet soils in full sun.') and MoBot's Water field reads Wet; that moisture requirement is carried by water_regime keep_moist, and MoBot adds 'Plants will not grow in standing water, but will tolerate some seasonal flooding.' The research record had set moisture_retentive on the prose alone; changed at landing under the structured-field-first drainage rule.

water_regime=keep_moist is based on MoBot's structured field "Water: Wet" plus its Culture requirement statement (boggy to wet soils); NC State has no structured watering field, only the Soil Drainage tag "Occasionally Wet" as corroboration.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figures found ("6 or more hours", "2-6 hours") are NC State's site-wide Light-field legend text, not species-specific prose, so per instructions they are not used.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source gives a species-specific fertilizing statement for Rosa palustris; genus-level rose-feeding guidance was deliberately excluded per instructions.

day/night temperature fields, humidity fields, light_fc fields, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, and the water day-interval/dry-down fields are all left null: no admissible source frames Rosa palustris care in these terms (it is an in-ground wetland shrub, not container/houseplant-managed).

RHS's page for Rosa palustris (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/16062/rosa-palustris/details, title confirmed as "Rosa palustris | swamp rose") contains only Botanical Details (Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Genus description, Name Status, Plant Range) with no Position, Soil, or pH sections to draw on.
No admissible source used the name "Marsh Rose" for this species; all three (NC State, MoBot, RHS) converge on "Swamp Rose"/"swamp rose".

records.name_note: NC State Extension's Common Name(s) field stacks five entries in alphabetical order — Possumhaw Viburnum, Smooth Witherod, Smooth Witherod Viburnum, Southern Wild Raisin, Wild Raisin — the same order as the page-title parenthetical, so its first entry is Possumhaw Viburnum. NC State's own Description prose opens with "Smooth Witherod." Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page (a separate dedicated single-species page) displays a single rendered "Common Name:" field reading "smooth witherod" (a longer Common Names list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's markup, so it is not quoted here), and its Noteworthy Characteristics prose separately states the plant "is also sometimes commonly called possumhaw viburnum" -- naming possumhaw viburnum as a secondary alternate, not MoBot's lead. So MoBot's rendered Common Name field leads with smooth witherod and NC State's Description prose opens with Smooth Witherod, while NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list opens with Possumhaw Viburnum; Smooth Witherod is used as common_name here, with Possumhaw Viburnum, Smooth Witherod Viburnum, Southern Wild Raisin, and Wild Raisin (per NC State) as documented alternates. Separately, NC State's structured "is often confused with" module lists Viburnum cassinoides -- a confusion note about a similar species, not a stated synonymy, and no admissible source consulted here asserted that V. cassinoides is treated as a variety of V. nudum, so no synonymy claim is made beyond disclosing this confusion note as the source states it. No RHS species page for Viburnum nudum was found (only cultivar pages), so scientific_name_accepted is left null. Distinct from Viburnum dentatum (Arrowwood Viburnum) and Viburnum prunifolium (Blackhaw Viburnum) already in this catalog.

records.name_note: All three sources converge on 'swamp azalea' as the species-distinguishing lead. NC State lists three common names in alphabetical order — Clammy Azalea, Swamp Azalea, Swamp Honeysuckle — the same order as the parenthetical in its page title, and each entry is a link to its own common-name index page under this species' URL; NC State's H1 is the bare binomial, and its Description prose opens 'The swamp azalea is a woody, broadleaf evergreen or deciduous shrub in the Ericaceae (blueberry) family and is native to the southern and eastern United states.' and uses the same name again in its culture paragraph. MoBot's Common Name field displays a single value, 'swamp azalea'; MoBot's body prose separately adds 'clammy azalea' (for the sticky corolla tubes) and 'honeysuckle azalea'. RHS's H1 is the bare binomial 'Rhododendron viscosum (Vs)' with 'swamp azalea' as the plant-profile subtitle directly beneath it, and lists 'swamp honeysuckle, white swamp honeysuckle' under a secondary Other common names heading. Because MoBot's single Common Name field and RHS's profile subtitle both designate 'swamp azalea' and NC State's body prose uses it as the working name, 'Swamp Azalea' is used as common_name; 'Clammy Azalea' and 'Swamp Honeysuckle' are real, sourced alternate names for this species but are not treated as the lead. Distinct from Rhododendron catawbiense, R. maximum, R. periclymenoides and R. simsii already in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (human-scoped) rates this species' poison characteristics as low severity. Its Poison Symptoms text reads: "While the plants are known to contain toxins, ingestion of moderate amounts of azalea (nectar or leaves) poses little toxic hazard." The Poison Toxic Principle is Grayanotoxins. The full Poison Part list (stacked values) is: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. NC State's Causes Contact Dermatitis field for this species reads No. The Plant Type list separately carries a "Poisonous" tag, and the Problems tags carry "Poisonous to Humans," "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" (the cat/dog/horse tags are separate structured fields from the human-scoped Poison block above). RHS corroborates pet-relevant risk with an unscoped-severity note: "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling," followed by a pets-specific line naming "Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, tortoises) Harmful if eaten." No admissible source gives a numeric toxic dose, and no source restricts the hazard to only fruit or only foliage - the poison-part list spans the whole plant.

records.name_note: Naming is split. NC State's Common Name(s) field carries eight alphabetized entries, the first of which, American Cyrilla, also opens the page title's parenthetical; NC State's own Description prose instead uses 'Swamp titi' throughout. MoBot's displayed Common Name field reads 'leatherwood', and its Noteworthy Characteristics prose calls the species 'leatherwood, black titi, or swamp cyrilla'. RHS's page header reads 'Cyrilla racemiflora | leatherwood', with 'black titi, myrtle' under Other common names. A UGA Extension multi-species publication (B 987) calls it 'Red Titi' in a single introductory sentence. This record leads with Leatherwood, the name MoBot's and RHS's dedicated pages both lead with, and discloses that NC State's list leads with American Cyrilla while its body prose uses Swamp titi. Note that 'Black Titi', one of the names NC State and RHS list for this species, is applied by UGA B987 to the separate species Cliftonia monophylla. 'Leatherwood' is also applied to the unrelated Dirca palustris, which is not in this catalog.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the only toxicity statement found in admissible sources (NC State) is scoped to honeybees — 'Toxic pollen from this plant is responsible for purple brood to honeybee colonies. This plant is not suitable for beekeepers.' — and names no cat or dog risk, so it cannot support a cats/dogs toxicity claim under the scoping rule. No admissible source carries a Poison Part/Poison Severity block for this species.

soil_ph left null in both directions: NC State's Soil pH field reads only 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended band that cannot supply a ceiling or floor on its own, and RHS's page for this species carries no pH field to check against in either direction (RHS's page here is thin — no Position, Soil, or pH data rendered, only a common-name subtitle and Other common names field).

soil_drainage set to moderate rather than moisture_retentive: NC State's structured Soil Drainage field itself lists Moist, Occasional Flooding, Occasionally Wet (no bare 'Good Drainage' tag), which read alone could suggest a wetter classification, but both NC State's own cultivation prose ('moist to wet well-drained sandy loam') and MoBot's Culture statement ('evenly moist to wet, well-draining...soils') explicitly require well-drained/well-draining conditions rather than consistently boggy soil, so the well-drained cultivation requirement controls and the token is moderate, not moisture_retentive.

water_regime set to keep_moist based on MoBot's and NC State's cultivation-level prose (both call for consistently moist-to-wet soil); disclosed against this is MoBot's own structured Water field, which reads the mid-scale 'Medium to wet' rather than a clean wet reading.
